newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: U.S. sees corruption threatening ties with Africa.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sees corruption threatening ties with Africa.

text.p: The United States said on Thursday its business and economic ties with some southern African nations were threatened by corruption and lack of transparency in awarding of major foreign contracts.

Lauri J. Fitz-Pegado, U.S. Assistant Secretary of Commerce, told the two-day regional trade and investment promotion conference in Zimbabwe that demands for bribes were a serious deterrent to new investment.
She said individual governments in the 12-member Southern African Development Community (SADC) must guarantee transparency in handling international tenders for big infrastructure projects.
Pegado, also the Director General, U.S. Foreign Commercial Service, said transparency was a key part of business transactions.

"I am particularly concerned that recent project awards could cause irreparable damage to the leaders and countries concerned and to our efforts to promote U.S. business interest here due to their lack of such transparency," she said.
Fitz-Pegado mentioned no names, but many delegates at the conference attended by more than 300 business executives and politicians said her finger was pointed at Zimbabwe.
A privatisation deal for the Hwange Thermal Power Station is mired in controversy after Zimbabwe's government ignored normal tender procedures and offered it to a Malaysian power producer.

President Robert Mugabe has defended the deal by saying he wanted other players other than Europeans to invest in his country. He sacked the entire 10-member board of the state Zimbabwe Electricity Supply Authority (ZESA) for demanding that the deal be passed through the tender board.
This was Zimbabwe's second highly controversial tender dispute this year after one over the establishment of a cellular telephone system.
On Wednesday, Chester Crocker, America's former assistant secretary of state for African affairs, also rounded up on the same issue when he addressed the Harare conference.
"Neither local or foreign investors will have the confidence to risk their capital if they perceive that awards and contracts are warped by political favouratism or improper dealings," he said.
"In the absence of a level playing field, they will look elsewhere or sit on their hands," he added.
